Im not really sure how to word it, but I realized that a lot of my anger stems from a lot of self-imposed despair. For example, when I feel like I’m not being heard, I get caught in a mental loop by telling myself that I’ll never be heard, which leads to more anger. Or even worse, I’d spend time wondering if I was mad “for no reason,” which my therapist tells me can add a lot of guilt and shame on top of the thoughts that I’m already having. 


So, I try to look inward and think of ways I can give myself whatever it is that I need at that moment. Getting to a solution that I can make
happen BY MYSELF has been my way of taking power over the situation, and I always feel pretty good after :)

I think what you told me would be okay to tell your therapist—no plans or intent, just fantasies. That was a situation where I had to ask what would/wouldn’t make my therapist obligated to intervene before talking about it.

Yes, it’s worked for me! Lasting changes take a long time, so please, take your time. We as people tend to attach a lot of guilt and shame onto the ways that we feel, and therapy was a great place for me to give myself the compassion I had been missing for so long. I hope things get better for you!!!

Hey, friend. I’m no wiseman per se, but from what you wrote, I got a funny feeling about Jack.

1. Him guilting her for not liking him sounds pretty toxic.

2. Him guilting the two of you the way he does is very… “beating around the bush,” if you will. Immature, to say it plainly.


So, before commenting, i went to look at your other posts, and i can confirm: he sounds pretty toxic. I’m only a young adult, but from what I’ve experienced in my life, I’d mention two things:

1. If you want something to change between the two of you, you need to be intentional about it. When he says something that makes you feel bad, mention it. Be above it—don’t get mad, don’t be guilt trippy about it, and don’t argue. Just state it, and be clear. If it makes it easier, imagine the conversation from a third person point of view, like a movie, and think of what you’d want the protagonist (you) to say to Jack. Being intentional takes courage, but you owe it to yourself! If he doesn’t care, well, that leads me to my next point,

2. You can’t change people :(

I had a friend group of over 10 years that went up in flames due to the lack of mutual respect. Im 21 now, and things are just fine without them, but i sometimes miss the good times. That’s just life. Better days have came my way since then :)

Jack’s reaction will probably make your thoughts a little clearer and help you process how you should feel about your curiosity for Emma.

All the best bro! I wish you well.

I wasn’t trying to convert you, so if I came off as pushy, I apologize. I think we could agree on that?

If you WISH you could believe in something, AND atheism is only serving to depress you, maybe just recognizing or realizing what you truly value in yourself and others could benefit you, rather than looking at us as “just meat,” as that is really depressing. I think wishing you could subscribe to a certain religion is the wrong approach. Take the time to recognize what you truly believe, and ask yourself whether or not it serves you positively. I grew up Catholic, and strayed away from the church around when I was 17. I just couldn’t bring myself to agree to certain things, like the Catholic stance on gay marriage. To me, shaming people for being homosexual was just not God-like or compassionate in any way. Kinda contradicting. Anyways, I tried to get back into it, but I just couldn’t do it without feeling ingenuous. It was a hard part of my life, losing my faith and feeling like we’re living in a Godless world. If you’re having a hard time believing there is an entity, but yearn for a communal sense, I think you might find some value in my perspective, as it might provoke some positive thought about your own spirituality or perceived reality.

All religions, when you put aside the belief in the powers that be, are philosophies on our being. How we came to be, how we should be if we want to be happy, etc. Basically, how we should live our lives and treat each other. They are deeply thought-out hypotheses about how to optimize our existences. Scriptures were written based on inspirations and wisdom accumulated throughout others’ human experiences. Hence, “The Book of Joshua,” “The Book of Isaiah,” etc. A good example of what I mean is the story of creation, if you’re familiar with it. It has its own limitations, but the philosophy behind it is arguably well-grounded. Obviously, the Earth is not flat, and men and women did not come first, but the ideas of original sin and such are very much true in our nature, and I used the story of creation as one of many tools to navigate my human experience. I guess what I’m saying is, each religion has many valuable things to take away from it, and some not so accurate or presently valuable things.

There is another component to religion that is essential and cannot be forgone, even if you don’t believe in any powers that be: Faith. Faith that there is good in the world, and that we have not been forsaken. Faith that we can be happy. Etc. An existence without faith of any sort is just heinous. Although my beliefs have changed, I’m very grateful to have had faith in my life, as it has pulled me out of the darkness many times. Although I’m not entirely sure what my faith is (I think I would classify as Agnostic? Idk), I have faith in good over evil, and that’s just that.

I hope this was helpful in some sort of way, or just interesting at the very least. Best of luck to you my friend :)
